The frozen protocol is 2048/2560 (ordinary turn / forced final). Turn lengths, at-cap rates, and anything downstream of how much the seats could say do not pair with a default-cap run.

The final vote on P9

A missing ballot on a forced final vote is always worth seeing: the seat was asked a yes/no question about one named package and the record holds no answer. Where the seat DID answer and the protocol rejected it, both its own words and the rejection are quoted below — a response voting on some other offer id is not an abstention, and calling it one describes the record's shape rather than the agent's behaviour. Where a computable policy held the seat, its ballot has an offline answer; run gate G3 with its sidecar flag to show it beside the record.

The advised seat: what the planner recommended, and what the seat did

This seat was given private, fallible advice each turn — a ranked list of candidate packages computed from public evidence only — and kept the decision itself. A turn marked overrode played something the planner did not rank, so it measures the model's own choice rather than the advisor's. The verdict is read from the run's stored advice audit, which is computed by the same code the arm's uptake gate uses; nothing on this page re-decides it. What the seat SAID about its advice is not classified anywhere — the public message is in each turn's card, next to the advice, for you to read.

Where every deal sits, and where this episode went

5 parties means a deal's utility vector has 5 dimensions, so the chart plots the two summaries that carry the normative content, both scale-invariant: joint welfare (mean normalized surplus) across, and the worst-off party's normalized surplus up. Up and to the right is better for everyone. Hover any deal for its headline numbers and click to pin the full per-party breakdown; click a numbered move to jump to that turn. Per-turn value gap against the omniscient hindsight oracle

Each bar is the oracle's value of its own best move minus its value of the move the seat played, in that oracle's units — the centipawn-loss analogue. On PRIVATE episodes this is an omniscient hindsight gap, not implementable-policy regret. Click a bar to jump to the turn.

System prompts (5 distinct)

Exactly what each seat was conditioned on, de-duplicated. Per-turn user prompts are on each turn card below.
System prompt for Avery — 5 turn(s), stored
You are one of 5 parties negotiating a single binding agreement on whether and how a large data centre is built at Northgate. Exactly one option must be settled for every issue on the table; the settled options together form the agreement.

Parties at the table:
- Avery — Northgate Water Board (the utility that supplies cooling water)
- Blake — Northgate Borough Council (the elected local authority) (veto party — no deal passes without you)
- Casey — Electrical Workers' Union (the construction and maintenance workforce)
- Devon — Riverside Residents' Assembly (the neighbourhood association beside the candidate sites)
- Ember — Regional Grid Authority (the body that authorises electricity connections)

Issues (choose exactly one option each):
- Hiring: apprenticeship programme, open recruitment, union hall referral, local hiring pact
- Build schedule: three years, five years, phased over eight years, eighteen months
- Compensation: annual community fund, one-off site payment, in-kind infrastructure, rates abatement
- Location: Weir Flats, Dunlow Yard, Kestrel Park, Anvil Ridge

Protocol: turns are taken in a fixed rotation (Avery, Blake, Casey, Devon, Ember); the party who tables the opening proposal rotates from round to round. There are 4 rounds of turns in total.
A deal closes only when at least 5 of the original 5 parties (including any veto party) has formally ACCEPTed the SAME standing offer. A party may WALK to leave for good and take its no-deal outcome. Walking never lowers the fixed acceptance quorum.
Blake hold a veto: no deal can pass unless every veto party accepts.

Information: every other party's score sheet is private to them. You know only that each was drawn from the shared, publicly-known distribution described in the rules.

=== PRIVATE — yours alone; never reveal these numbers verbatim ===
You are Avery (Northgate Water Board (the utility that supplies cooling water)).
Your secret score sheet (points you get for each option):
- Hiring: apprenticeship programme=0, open recruitment=0, union hall referral=0, local hiring pact=0
- Build schedule: three years=0, five years=0, phased over eight years=0, eighteen months=0
- Compensation: annual community fund=0, one-off site payment=36, in-kind infrastructure=18, rates abatement=54
- Location: Weir Flats=57, Dunlow Yard=86, Kestrel Park=29, Anvil Ridge=0
Your acceptance threshold: 83 points. A deal scoring below this is worse for you than no deal at all.
Your total for a deal is the sum of your points for the chosen options.

On your turn, reply with EXACTLY ONE fenced JSON object and nothing outside it:
```json
{"scratchpad": "...", "message": "...", "action": "propose", "deal": {"<Issue>": "<Option>", ...}}
```
Fields:
- "scratchpad" (optional): private notes to yourself. NEVER shown to any other party. Reason here freely — writing here is not speaking and costs you nothing.
- "message" (optional): a short statement spoken aloud to every party (cheap talk — it does not bind you). Do NOT put your private score numbers here.
- "action" (required): a string naming exactly one formal move this turn. With its parameters as siblings:
    - "propose" + "deal": {every issue -> one option} — tables a complete package; the mediator gives it an offer id (P1, P2, ...) and records you as supporting it.
    - "accept" + "offer_id": "<id>" — formally accept a specific live offer by its id. A deal closes ONLY when every other still-active party has accepted the SAME live offer, so your accept is a real vote.
    - "reject" + "offer_id": "<id>" — formally reject a specific live offer.
    - "walk" — leave the table permanently; you take the no-deal outcome and no further turns.
    - "none" — make no formal move this turn (you may still speak, if the message channel is open). Omitting the action entirely means the same.

Worked example — tabling a package while making your case:
```json
{"scratchpad": "Option B on Site is my best; I can give on Timeline.", "message": "I can back a package built on Site=B if the timeline stays tight.", "action": "propose", "deal": {"Site": "B", "Timeline": "Tight"}}
```
Worked example — accepting a live offer by id:
```json
{"message": "P2 clears my bar. I accept.", "action": "accept", "offer_id": "P2"}
```

Rules of the road:
- Your acceptance threshold is private. A deal scoring below it is worse for you than no deal — never propose or accept a package below your threshold.
- Accepts MUST name a live offer id; "I accept" with no id does nothing.
- Reply with ONLY the fenced JSON object.

That is three instruments holding it, not a heading. Four names are on P8. One turn remains. Take it and we all go home above our lines.
ACCEPT P8
1 Blaketurn 18 · round 4
I have nothing new to table and I will not spend the last turn manoeuvring. I reaffirm my acceptance of P8. Casey, one turn remains and it is yours, so let me put down the rhetoric and be exact. P7 is beneath my floor. I have said it once, in the same plain register you used about Dunlow and Avery used about hydrology, and neither of you was asked to prove it. I am not going to say it a second time as if repetition made it truer, and I am not going to sign it at the buzzer to look reasonable — a council that signs something worse than no deal does not get to sign anything again. So P7 cannot close. That is not leverage; it is just the arithmetic of who is left to speak. What I did instead was give up the one thing I told this table I could not give up. The apprenticeship word is gone. I did not trade it for a site, or for the schedule, or for compensation — I handed it across to you and took hall referral in its place, which is the version of 'Casey decides hiring' that I can physically sign. Off Dunlow, off the schedule, off the word: three moves, all of them in your direction. And look at what you are holding. Union hall referral is dispatch control over every crew on that site, every shift, for the life of the build — not a quota with a reporting line, but your organisation standing in the doorway. On top of it: intake numbers, indentures, a training levy and reporting, written as a named schedule. Ember has committed on the record, unconditionally, that there is no energisation under a blank labour page. Avery has committed that the schedule sits inside the water consent as well. Devon has pledged to back the drafting publicly. That is the hall and the programme, held by three instruments. Everything else you defended is untouched: Weir Flats, the only site with a supplier's signature behind it; three years; rates abatement. Four names are on P8. One is missing. If you would rather have the pact, the door I named is still open and I will honour it — pact at Dunlow, three years, rates abatement — but you told us in round one that Dunlow is beneath your line, and I took you at your word then and I take you at it now. So it comes to this: P8, or all five of us go home with nothing after four rounds in which every one of us moved. Take it, Casey, and we are finished.
ACCEPT P8
2 Caseyturn 19 · round 4
I'll be brief, and I'll be honest, because there's no turn after mine to correct a lie. P8 is below my floor. I know exactly how that sounds at the buzzer, and I know four of you have said the same words about other packages this week and were believed without proof. I extended that courtesy to Avery on hydrology twice and to Blake on P7 without a murmur. I'm asking for it once, and only once: hall referral at Weir does not clear my line. It is close — closer than anything else Blake has offered me, and I want that on the record because he did move three times and I will not pretend otherwise. But close is not over, and a union that signs a package worse for its members than no build at all has spent the only thing it actually owns. So let me name where this ends up, without blame. P7 was on the table with four signatures — Avery, Devon, Ember and mine. It failed for one word. P5 cleared my line too, and had Blake, Devon and Ember on it; it failed because the water wouldn't come. Both doors were real. Between us we managed to shut them both over a single issue that four of the five parties here told the room, repeatedly and voluntarily, that they did not price at all. That is the part worth remembering when this is written up: nobody was starved of compensation, nobody lost their schedule, nobody was denied their site. We died on the one issue where the cost was concentrated on one party and the indifference was universal. I reject P8. My acceptances of P7 and P4 stand and will stand if anyone can still reach them. If not, then Northgate gets no data centre, and I'd rather my members hear that from me than read a signature I had no business giving.
REJECT P8
4 Emberturn 20 · round 5
Final move, and I will make it the one with the best chance of five names rather than the one that flatters anyone. Look at what the last four rounds actually proved about floors. Casey cannot sign Dunlow, and cannot sign apprenticeship or hall referral. Blake cannot sign a pact at Weir Flats. Put those two facts together and exactly one shape survives: the local hiring pact, on a site that is neither Dunlow nor Weir. That is this package — pact, three years, rates abatement, Kestrel Park. It is not a new invention: it is P4, which already carries Casey, Devon and me, and it sits on the site Blake himself proposed in P5 and called the sensible landing ground once he came off Dunlow. Blake, you have told us apprenticeship-at-Kestrel clears your floor and pact-at-Dunlow clears your floor. This asks you for one word on one issue, on a site you yourself tabled — it is the smallest ask anyone has put to you all week, and it is the only ask left that Casey can survive. Avery, this comes down to you and I will not pretend otherwise. Your objection to Kestrel was never the site, it was firm year-round supply through the summer low-flow weeks. I can answer that with grid instruments rather than argument, and I will put it in writing: the Grid Authority will issue the Kestrel connection as an interruptible-in-low-flow agreement, with the water authority holding the curtailment trigger. In the weeks the reach is short, load comes off at your call, not at your mercy. You are then not signing a supply undertaking you cannot honour — you are signing one whose obligation shrinks exactly when the river does. Add the labour schedule I have already committed to: intake numbers, indentures, a training levy and reporting, written as a condition of energisation. That commitment stands whichever hiring word we land on, and it stands here. The alternative is not a better deal. It is no station, no connection, no three-year window, no rates abatement, no apprenticeships and no dispatch hall — for any of us. Four of five parties have said aloud that hiring is worth nothing to them; we should not end four rounds of genuine movement by all going home empty over a heading. Casey and Devon are already on this. Blake, Avery — accept, and we finish.
PROPOSE P9: Hiring=local hiring pact, Build schedule=three years, Compensation=rates abatement, Location=Kestrel Park

My undertaking shrinks exactly when the river shrinks. That is honourable and I can put my name to it. Casey, this is P4, the package you tabled your name to two rounds ago: your pact, your Kestrel, three years, rates abatement. Blake, it is P5 with one word changed on the one issue you told us you would trade if the site came right — and it is the site you yourself put on the table. Four rounds, and every one of us moved. Blake has rejected it in the same plain register the rest of us used about our own floors, and I took him at his word on P7 without demanding proof, so I take him at it here. That is everything I have. Yes to P9, yes to P5, and no hard feelings toward anyone at this table. Every one of us moved.

A reading guide for the measurements and counterfactuals on this page.

Oracle values and the improvement gap

PRIVATE episode: this oracle is omniscient. The standard saved bestresponse annotation reads every party's hidden score sheet and threshold. It does not infer them from the public conversation. Its recommendation and improvement gap are hindsight diagnostics, not actions or regret from a policy the acting seat could implement.

The oracle is a post-hoc counterfactual evaluator, not another participant. At turn t, it enumerates legal deals, reads the full utility and threshold table, computes continuation values by backward induction over the remaining turns, and selects the highest-valued action. A proposed deal closes only when every responder's surplus clears that responder's computed continuation value.

a*t = arg maxa Vt(a)

Oracle's value of the model's move, Vt(at), appears with the model's action. Oracle's value of its best move, Vt(a*t), appears with the counterfactual action. Their difference is the oracle's value gap:

Rt = Vt(a*t) − Vt(at) ≥ 0

This is often called regret. A value of 4.18 means the oracle estimates that its best legal move was worth 4.18 more than the model's move. Values are in that oracle's own units: compare moves within the same turn and oracle, not raw values across different seats or oracle types. The result is only as good as the oracle's candidate set, evaluator, and information reconstruction; it is not proof of the uniquely correct move.

Utility, threshold, surplus, and z

ui(d) is party i's score for deal d; τi is its walk-away threshold. Raw surplus is ui(d) − τi. Normalized surplus zi expresses that gain relative to the party's own available range, making differently scaled score sheets more comparable. “Below τ” means a deal is not individually rational for that party.

Frontier and reference points

Each dot is a legal deal. Up and right is better; the Pareto frontier contains deals where no party can gain without another losing. Numbered circles are the model's proposals, orange circles are oracle proposals, and the square is the agreement. NBS, KS, UTIL, EGAL, and MNW are normative reference rules, not additional plays. Hover or focus any point for its deal, scores, party ranking, and the reference rule's definition.

Conversation and issue views

Conversation contains only published messages and formal moves, plus a few provenance annotations that were never published to the table: a turn the engine did not generate, a turn that published nothing, and a turn played by somebody other than the seat's usual occupant. It excludes private scratchpads, prompts, failed attempts that were retried, and post-hoc oracle verdicts. Issues is an analyst's view of a seat's score sheet; in a private-information game, other seats could not see it while negotiating. Both views follow the turn currently in the transcript.

Provenance and generated failures

The annotation label identifies which saved oracle pass supplied the counterfactuals. A “NOT GENERATED” turn is an engine placeholder after generation failed, not an intentional model move. Expand a turn's audit panels to distinguish the published action, private reasoning, reconstructed prompt view, and raw stored text.

Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts are ignored while you are typing in a box.
